title: Exercise and rest: why muscles get tired, and what sleep does

summary.text: Squeeze a clothes peg again and again, and your fingers slow down and start to ache. Rest for two minutes, and much of their strength comes back. A working muscle uses up its quick store of fuel. Your blood brings oxygen so the muscle can refill that store, and carries waste away. Regular exercise makes muscles, the heart and bones stronger. Yoga, an old Indian practice of poses and slow breathing, keeps the body bendy and steady. Sleep is the longest rest of all. While you sleep, your body grows and repairs itself, and your brain stays busy, sorting what you learned and making dreams. A child of 8 needs about 9 to 12 hours of sleep every night.
summary.art: A child squeezing a clothes peg at a table, a small timer beside her. Next to it, the same child asleep in bed under a window with stars, with soft dream bubbles above her head.

intro.hook: Try this. Hold a full one-litre water bottle in one hand. Stretch your arm straight out to the side, at shoulder height. At first it feels light. Keep holding. After a minute your arm shakes and burns. The bottle did not get any heavier. So what changed?
intro.text: What changed was inside your arm. The muscles holding the bottle were working hard without a break. In this unit you find out what a muscle uses up when it works, and what rest gives back. You also find out what exercise does to your body over weeks, and what your body and brain do while you sleep.
intro.art: A child standing with one arm stretched out sideways holding a water bottle, the arm starting to tremble, and a wall clock behind.

outcomes: I can explain that a working muscle uses up its quick store of fuel, and that blood brings oxygen to help refill it while I rest.
I can run a fair test of how a muscle gets tired and how rest helps, and show my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can name three kinds of exercise, for stamina, strength and flexibility, and give an example of each.
I can do three yoga poses and slow breathing, and say what yoga helps the body to do.
I can say how much sleep a child of my age needs, and describe what the body and brain do during sleep.
I can tell how scientists found out, in 1953, that the brain stays busy during sleep.
I can plan a day with enough exercise, rest and sleep, and explain my plan.

terms.meaning: A part of the body that moves you by pulling. Muscles are made of long, thin cells joined in bundles.
terms.example: The muscles in your forearm pull on your fingers when you squeeze a clothes peg.
terms.art: An arm with the skin drawn see-through, showing the bundles of red muscle running from the elbow to the fingers.

terms.meaning: When a muscle contracts, it gets shorter and fatter, and pulls on a bone.
terms.example: Bend your arm and feel the muscle at the front of your upper arm get hard. It has contracted.
terms.art: A child bending one arm, with the upper arm muscle bulging.

terms.meaning: When a muscle relaxes, it stops pulling and goes soft and long again.
terms.example: Let your arm hang down. The muscle at the front of your upper arm is soft. It has relaxed.
terms.art: The same child with the arm hanging straight down, the muscle soft.

terms.meaning: Fatigue is tiredness. A muscle with fatigue works more slowly and more weakly, and may ache.
terms.example: After two minutes of squeezing a peg, your fingers slow down. That is muscle fatigue.
terms.art: A hand squeezing a clothes peg, with the fingers drawn shaking and small lines showing an ache.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air. You breathe it in, and your blood carries it to every part of your body.
terms.example: When you run, you breathe faster to take in more oxygen.
terms.art: A child breathing in, with small dots of air going into the lungs and red blood carrying them to the legs.

terms.meaning: How long you can keep going at a hard activity before you need to stop.
terms.example: Skipping with a rope for five minutes without stopping takes stamina.
terms.art: A girl skipping with a rope, the rope a blur, a timer beside her.

terms.meaning: How hard your muscles can push or pull.
terms.example: Carrying a bucket of water up the stairs takes strength.
terms.art: A child carrying a small bucket of water up a flight of stairs in a block of flats.

terms.meaning: How far your body can bend and stretch without pain.
terms.example: Sitting on the floor with straight legs and touching your toes takes flexibility.
terms.art: A child sitting on the floor with straight legs, reaching for the toes.

terms.meaning: An old Indian practice of body poses, slow breathing and paying attention. A yoga pose is called an asana.
terms.example: Standing on one leg in tree pose, called vrikshasana, is yoga.
terms.art: A child in tree pose on a mat, one foot resting on the other leg, hands joined above the head.

terms.meaning: The breathing part of yoga. You breathe in and out slowly, in a set way.
terms.example: Breathing in for a count of four and out for a count of six is a simple pranayama.
terms.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed, a hand on the belly rising with the breath.

terms.meaning: During a night, sleep goes round in cycles. Each cycle has light sleep, deep sleep and dreaming sleep, and lasts about one and a half hours in older children and adults.
terms.example: In ten hours of sleep, you go round the cycle about six or seven times.
terms.art: A circle path drawn over a sleeping child, with three parts marked light, deep and dreaming.

terms.meaning: The part of sleep when most vivid dreams happen. The eyes dart about under the closed eyelids. REM stands for rapid eye movement.
terms.example: If you wake from dreaming sleep, you can often remember a dream.
terms.art: A sleeping face, with small arrows showing the eyes moving under the closed lids.

terms.meaning: A soft, springy pad between two bones of your backbone. It holds water like a sponge.
terms.example: The discs in your back get slightly squashed during the day and fill up again at night, while you lie down.
terms.art: A side view of a few backbone bones stacked up, with soft round pads between them.

explanations.concept: What a working muscle uses up
explanations.definition: A muscle needs energy to contract. It keeps a small, quick store of fuel inside its cells. To refill that store, the muscle needs oxygen and food, which the blood brings.
explanations.description: When you squeeze a peg fast, your finger muscles contract again and again. Each contraction uses some of the quick fuel store. If you keep going without a break, the muscle uses the fuel faster than the blood can help refill it. Waste also builds up inside the muscle. So the muscle slows down and starts to ache. When you stop, blood keeps flowing through the muscle. It brings oxygen, and the muscle uses it to refill its store. It also carries the waste away. After a short rest the muscle can work hard again. The quick fuel is called phosphocreatine. It was found in 1927 by Cyrus Fiske and Yellapragada Subbarow, who grew up in Andhra Pradesh, and at the same time by Grace and Philip Eggleton in England.
examples: Squeezing a peg for two and a half minutes without stopping, your count falls in every round.
After a short rest, a fast bowler can run in and bowl hard again.
Carrying a heavy bag up three floors, your legs ache by the top. After a minute of standing, they feel better.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a finger muscle with a small fuel tank inside the muscle cells emptying, and a red blood vessel beside it bringing oxygen dots in.
explanations.context: This card says what a muscle uses when it works, and what blood does while the muscle rests.

explanations.concept: Why muscles get tired: two answers
explanations.description: Everyone agrees that a muscle that works hard without rest slows down. Scientists still argue about what causes most of the tiredness. One answer is that it happens inside the muscle. The other answer is that the brain makes you slow down early, to keep you safe. Most scientists now think both happen.
examples: In the peg test, the fingers slow down even though you try your hardest.
Runners near the end of a race can often sprint the last 100 metres. Their muscles still had fuel left.

perspectives.explanation: Tiredness comes mainly from inside the muscle. The quick fuel store runs low, and waste builds up inside the cells. This makes each contraction weaker.

perspectives.who: Tim Noakes, a South African sports scientist, and others
perspectives.explanation: Much of the tiredness is made by the brain. The brain feels the warning signs and makes the body slow down long before the muscle is harmed. That is why people can speed up at the finish line.

explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: on the left, a muscle with an almost empty fuel tank, and on the right, a brain with a small hand on a brake lever.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: what exactly makes a muscle tired.

explanations.concept: How exercise makes a body stronger
explanations.definition: Exercise is moving your body hard enough to breathe faster and get warm. Done often, over weeks, it makes muscles stronger, the heart and lungs better at their work, and bones harder.
explanations.description: A muscle that works hard often grows a little bigger and stronger. A heart that is often made to beat fast grows stronger too, so it can pump more blood in each beat. Bones get harder when they carry weight and get jolted, as in running, jumping and climbing. Astronauts in space float, so their bones and muscles carry no weight. They get weaker unless the astronauts exercise for about two hours every day. There are three main kinds of exercise. Stamina exercise, such as skipping, cycling, swimming and kho-kho, works the heart and lungs. Strength exercise, such as climbing, carrying and pushing, works the muscles and bones. Flexibility exercise, such as yoga and stretching, keeps the body bending easily. Many games, such as kabaddi, use all three.
examples: Climbing the stairs of your building every day builds stamina and strength.
A child who skips every day for a month can usually skip for longer without stopping than at the start.
Astronauts on the International Space Station run on a treadmill strapped down with belts, so their bones keep getting jolts.
explanations.art: Three panels: a girl skipping (stamina), a boy carrying a bucket up stairs (strength), and a girl stretching on a mat (flexibility).
explanations.context: This card is about what exercise does to your body when you do it often, over weeks and months.

explanations.definition: Yoga is an old Indian practice. It has three main parts: poses called asanas, slow breathing called pranayama, and paying close attention to the body and the mind.
explanations.description: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali is an old book about yoga. It was written in Sanskrit between about 1,600 and 2,200 years ago. Nobody knows the exact date. It says a pose should be steady and comfortable. Many of the yoga poses taught around the world today come from Tirumalai Krishnamacharya, who taught yoga in Mysuru from the 1930s. One of his first women students was Indra Devi. She had been born in Latvia, and she later taught yoga in China, the United States and Argentina. Today, studies find that regular yoga helps people bend further and balance better. Since 2015, 21 June has been the International Day of Yoga.
examples: Cobra pose, bhujangasana, bends the back gently backwards.
Child's pose, balasana, is a resting pose with the forehead on the floor.
explanations.art: A family doing yoga on mats on a small balcony in the morning, a grandmother in tree pose, a child in cobra pose.
explanations.context: This card says what yoga is, where it comes from, and what it does for the body.

explanations.definition: Sleep is a long, regular rest in which you lie still and your senses notice much less. Every night it goes round in cycles of light sleep, deep sleep and dreaming sleep.
explanations.description: In deep sleep, your breathing and heartbeat slow down. This is when the body releases most of its growth hormone, a chemical messenger that helps children grow and helps the body repair itself. In dreaming sleep, also called REM sleep, the brain is nearly as busy as when you are awake. Your eyes dart about under your eyelids, and most vivid dreams happen. Your arm and leg muscles go floppy, so you do not act out your dreams. Sleep also helps you remember. People who sleep after learning something new remember it better the next day than people who stay awake. A child aged 6 to 12 needs about 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night.
examples: A baby sleeps for most of the day and night.
After a good night's sleep, a dance step practised yesterday often feels easier.
A dog asleep may twitch their paws and whimper during dreaming sleep.
explanations.art: A sleeping child with a simple wave line above her, slow and big for deep sleep, then quick and small for dreaming sleep.
explanations.context: This card says what the body and brain do during a night's sleep.

explanations.concept: Why do we sleep at all?
explanations.description: Nearly every animal that has been studied sleeps or rests in a sleep-like way, even fruit flies and tiny worms. Sleep must matter a great deal, because a sleeping animal is easier to catch. Scientists have several ideas about why sleep is needed, and nobody has the full answer yet. Sleep may give the body time to repair and grow. It may help the brain sort and store memories. It may help the brain clear away waste made during the day. That last idea comes from studies on mice, and scientists are still testing it.
examples: Dolphins sleep with one half of their brain at a time, so they can keep swimming up to breathe.
Frigatebirds can sleep for a few seconds at a time while they fly over the sea.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study growth and repair
perspectives.explanation: Sleep is when the body rebuilds. Growth hormone is released mostly in deep sleep.
Sleep is when the brain replays and stores what was learned during the day.
During sleep, fluid may wash waste out of the brain. This was seen in mice in 2013, and newer studies disagree about it.

explanations.art: A sleeping fruit fly, a dolphin with one eye open, and a frigatebird gliding over the sea, each with a small moon above.
explanations.context: This card is about a question nobody has fully answered: why animals need to sleep at all.

explanations.concept: Why you are taller in the morning
explanations.definition: Between the bones of your backbone are soft pads called discs. They hold water. Standing and sitting all day squeezes some water out, so you get a little shorter. Lying down at night lets them soak it back up.
explanations.description: Most people are about half a centimetre to one centimetre taller just after waking up than at bedtime. Most of the height is lost in the first hour or two after getting up. Astronauts in space have no weight pressing down on their backs. Their discs fill up and their backbones straighten a little, so they grow up to about 5 centimetres taller. They shrink back after they return to Earth.
examples: Measure yourself at bedtime and again just after waking. The morning mark is usually a little higher.
A sponge squeezed in your hand gets thinner. Put it in water and it swells again.
explanations.art: Two pencil marks on a wall beside a child, one labelled night and one a little higher labelled morning.
explanations.context: This card explains a surprising fact about rest: lying down at night makes you a little taller.

agreed.text: A muscle that works hard without a break gets slower and weaker, and rest lets it recover.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can see it with the peg test at home. Scientists measure it with machines that record muscle force.

agreed.text: Working muscles need oxygen, which the blood brings. When less blood reaches a muscle, it tires faster.
agreed.evidence: Squeezing a peg with the arm held up, so less blood reaches the hand, tires the fingers faster. Lab studies that squeeze the blood supply with a cuff show the same.

agreed.text: Regular exercise makes muscles, bones, the heart and the lungs stronger.
agreed.evidence: Studies follow children and adults for months and measure their fitness and bone strength. Astronauts lose bone and muscle without exercise.

agreed.text: Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night.
agreed.evidence: In 2016, a group of sleep doctors in the United States studied hundreds of research papers and agreed on these numbers.

agreed.text: The brain is very busy during sleep, especially in dreaming sleep.
agreed.evidence: Machines that record the brain's electrical signals show it. This was first seen clearly in 1953.

challenging.claim: The ache the day after hard exercise is caused by lactic acid left in the muscles.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among sports coaches and parents
challenging.for: Working muscles do make lactic acid, and lactic acid was for a long time blamed for tiredness.
challenging.against: Lactic acid is cleared from the muscles within about an hour after exercise. The ache the next day comes from tiny injuries in the muscle, which heal and make it stronger.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea that turned out to be wrong: what causes the ache the day after exercise.

challenging.claim: Most tiredness during exercise is made by the brain, not by the muscle.
challenging.who: Tim Noakes, a South African sports scientist, and others
challenging.for: People can often speed up at the end of a race, so their muscles had more left.
challenging.against: The peg test shows the muscle itself slowing down. Lab tests show the muscle's fuel store falling.
challenging.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: is tiredness in the muscle or in the brain?

challenging.claim: You can make up for lost sleep in the week by sleeping late on Sunday.
challenging.for: Sleeping longer after a short night does help you feel less sleepy.
challenging.against: Studies find that one long sleep does not undo all the effects of a week of short nights. A steady bedtime works better.
challenging.context: This card is about whether lost sleep can be made up later.

challenging.claim: Resting is a waste of time.
challenging.who: A common feeling, among busy children and grown-ups
challenging.for: While you rest, you are not getting anything visible done.
challenging.against: In the peg test, two minutes of rest brought back much of the strength. In deep sleep, the body releases growth hormone. Rest is when the body refills, repairs and grows.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that resting achieves nothing.

big_questions.q: After two minutes of rest, your peg count went up again. Where did the strength come back from?
big_questions.hint: Think about what kept flowing through your hand while it rested.

big_questions.q: Your body lies still for 10 hours every night. Is sleep a time of doing nothing?
big_questions.hint: Think of growing, dreaming and remembering. Which of them happen while you sleep?

big_questions.q: Tiredness is a feeling. Does it come from the muscle or from the brain?
big_questions.hint: Runners can often sprint at the finish line. What does that tell you?

big_questions.q: Your heart beats your whole life. It rests for a moment between every beat. Is there anything in the world that works without ever resting?
big_questions.hint: Think of day and night, the tide, a plant at night, and your breath.

big_questions.q: When you dream, where are you?
big_questions.hint: Your body is in bed. What about the you that runs and talks in the dream?

story.title: The Night Before Pongal
story.note: Lakshmi, her family and her dance teacher are made up. What the story shows is true: tired muscles need rest to work well, and sleep helps people remember a new skill.
text: Lakshmi was nine, and she lived on the fourth floor of a block of flats in Chennai. In three days, her dance class would dance at the Pongal function in the building's courtyard. Lakshmi had a new part, right at the front. It was a quick, stamping step called a jathi, and she could not get it right.
'Feet together, then out, stamp, stamp, turn,' said Revathi Miss at the evening class. 'Your feet must land exactly on the beat, Lakshmi. Practise slowly at home. Then sleep well.'

Lakshmi did not practise slowly. She practised fast, and she practised a lot. After dinner she stamped up and down the hall until the downstairs aunty knocked on the ceiling with a broom. Then she practised on the soft rug in her room, where the stamping made no sound. Her little brother Arjun sat on the bed and copied her with his hands.
At ten o'clock, Amma looked in. 'Lights off, Lakshmi.'
'Five more minutes,' said Lakshmi.

At eleven, Amma looked in again. Lakshmi was still stamping. Her legs were shaking now. The front of her thighs burned. Every time she tried the turn, she wobbled. The more she practised, the worse it got.
'I am getting worse,' said Lakshmi, and she felt like crying. 'I practised for two hours, and I am getting worse.'
Paati, her grandmother, was sitting in the doorway, folding clothes. She was seventy-two, and she still did yoga every morning on the balcony.

'Come here,' said Paati. 'Squeeze my hand as hard as you can.' Lakshmi squeezed. 'Again. Again. Faster.' After twenty squeezes, Lakshmi's hand was slow and aching. 'Now put your hand on your knee and wait,' said Paati. She folded two more saris. Then she held out her hand. 'Squeeze.' Lakshmi squeezed, and this time it was strong again.
'Your hand did nothing for two minutes,' said Paati. 'So why is it strong again?'
Lakshmi frowned. 'Because it rested?'

'Because while it rested, it was busy,' said Paati. 'Your blood was flowing through it all the time, filling it up again. Your legs are like your hand. They are empty now. Stamping more will not fill them.'
'But I still don't know the step,' said Lakshmi.
'Then go to sleep,' said Paati. 'While you sleep, your brain goes over what you practised today. Many times, I have learned a hard pose in the evening and found it easier in the morning.'

Lakshmi did not believe her. But she was too tired to argue. She lay down. She thought she would lie awake worrying. The next thing she knew, the sun was coming through the window and the crows were calling.

She stood up. Her legs felt a little stiff, but they were not shaking any more. She went to the rug, slowly, and tried the step. Feet together, then out, stamp, stamp, turn. Her feet knew where to go. She did it again, a little faster. She did not wobble on the turn.
'Paati!' she shouted. 'It's in my feet!'
Arjun woke up and came to look. 'Teach me,' he said.
So Lakshmi taught him, slowly, the way Revathi Miss had said. Feet together, then out, stamp, stamp, turn. 'Not fast,' she told him. 'Get it right slowly. Then stop and rest. Then sleep on it.'
That evening at class, Revathi Miss watched Lakshmi do the step three times. 'What happened?' she asked. 'Yesterday your feet were everywhere.'
'I slept,' said Lakshmi.
Revathi Miss laughed. 'That is the hardest practice of all for some people.'

On Pongal day, the courtyard was full. The pongal pot bubbled over, and everyone shouted 'Pongalo pongal!' Then the dancers came out. Lakshmi was at the front. Her feet landed exactly on the beat. In the second row of the audience, Arjun was doing the step with his hands, and Paati was keeping time with her fingers on her knee.
That night, Lakshmi went to bed at nine o'clock without being asked. Amma was so surprised that she checked whether Lakshmi had a fever.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Lakshmi's legs were tired because her muscles had used up their quick fuel faster than her blood could help refill it. More practice in that state only made her wobble more. When Paati made her squeeze, rest and squeeze again, Lakshmi felt the strength come back after two minutes of rest. Sleep did two jobs. Her muscles recovered, and her brain went over the new movement, so the step felt easier in the morning. Studies find that sleeping after practising a new movement helps people do it better the next day.
ask: Why did Lakshmi get worse the longer she practised?
Why was Lakshmi's hand strong again after resting on her knee for two minutes?
What did Paati say Lakshmi's brain would do while she slept?
Lakshmi taught Arjun to practise slowly, then rest, then sleep. Why is that good advice?
Paati is seventy-two and still does yoga every morning. What do you think yoga gives her?

games.title: Day and Night: the energy race
games.context: This is a board game about one whole day, from waking up to sleeping. Players answer questions about exercise, rest and sleep, and keep their energy up until bedtime.

printables.title: A board with 24 squares, one for each hour, going round in a circle from 6 in the morning
items: Square 1: 6 a.m., wake up
Squares 4, 10 and 16: PLAY! Do 10 star jumps or march on the spot, then gain 1 energy
Squares 7 and 13: TOO LONG ON A SCREEN. Lose 1 energy
Squares 9 and 18: REST. Take three slow breaths, then gain 1 energy
Square 15: BIG GAME OF KHO-KHO. Lose 2 energy, but move on 2 squares
Square 22: BEDTIME
Squares 23 and 24: DEEP SLEEP and DREAMING SLEEP

printables.title: 24 question cards to cut out
items: What happens to your peg count if you squeeze without a break? (It goes down)
What brings oxygen to a working muscle? (The blood)
Does rest help a tired muscle recover? (Yes)
How many hours of sleep does a child of 8 need? (About 9 to 12)
Name a stamina exercise. (Skipping, cycling, swimming, kho-kho or running)
Name a strength exercise. (Climbing, carrying, wall push-ups)
Name a flexibility exercise. (Yoga or stretching)
What is a yoga pose called? (An asana)
What is the breathing part of yoga called? (Pranayama)
Name the yoga pose where you stand on one leg. (Tree pose, vrikshasana)
In which part of sleep do most vivid dreams happen? (Dreaming sleep, or REM sleep)
Do your eyes move during dreaming sleep? (Yes, they dart about under the eyelids)
Does the brain switch off when you sleep? (No, it stays busy)
When is most growth hormone released? (In deep sleep)
Are you taller at bedtime or in the morning? (In the morning)
Why do astronauts exercise every day? (So their bones and muscles don't get weaker)
Who discovered dreaming sleep in 1953? (Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman)
Does a raised hand tire faster or slower when squeezing a peg? (Faster)
Does the heart rest between beats? (Yes, for a moment between every beat)
Which day is the International Day of Yoga? (21 June)
TRY IT: stand in tree pose for 10 seconds. Did you do it?
TRY IT: hum like a bee for one long breath out.
TRY IT: squeeze your fists tight, then let go. Which feels better?
TRY IT: touch your toes slowly and hold for three breaths.

printables.title: One counter for each player, and 5 energy tokens each

rules: Each player starts on square 1, 6 a.m., with 3 energy tokens.
On your turn, another player reads you a question card. Playing alone? Read it yourself and check the answer in brackets.
Answer right, and roll the dice and move that many squares. Answer wrong, and move 1 square.
On a TRY IT card, do it. Then gain 1 energy and roll.
Follow what the square says. You can never have more than 5 energy tokens.
If your energy reaches 0, you must REST: miss one turn and gain 2 energy.
When you reach BEDTIME, stop there. The game ends when everyone reaches bedtime. The player with the most energy left wins. Then everyone says one thing their body does during sleep.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the board. 2. Give each player a counter and 3 energy tokens. 3. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: This board is one whole day, from waking up to bedtime. You need energy to get through it. Let's see who reaches bedtime with the most energy left.
flow.kid: Put your counter on 6 a.m. Take 3 energy tokens. Mix up the cards. Can you reach bedtime with energy left?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Day and Night game. Here you set up the board.

flow.do: Play the card 'Does rest help a tired muscle recover?' as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card. Does rest help a tired muscle recover?
flow.kid: Practice card. Does rest help a tired muscle recover? Tap your answer.

check.q: Does rest help a tired muscle recover?
options: Yes, blood refills it with what it needs
No, a tired muscle stays tired all day
check.why: While a muscle rests, blood keeps flowing through it. The blood brings oxygen, and the muscle uses it to refill its quick fuel. That is why your peg count rose after two minutes of rest.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Do every PLAY, REST and TRY IT square for real.
flow.say: Answer, roll and move. When you land on PLAY, really do it!
flow.kid: Answer your card. Roll and move. On PLAY squares, really do the star jumps!
flow.parent: In a flat with neighbours below, swap star jumps for marching on the spot. Most games last about 10 to 15 minutes.

flow.do: When everyone reaches bedtime, each player says one thing the body does during sleep.
flow.say: Everyone is in bed. Tell me one thing your body or brain is doing while you sleep.
flow.kid: You reached bedtime. Say one thing your body does while you sleep.

ask.q: What does your body do while you sleep?
good: It grows, because growth hormone is released in deep sleep.
The brain sorts what I learned.
The discs in my back fill up, so I am taller in the morning.

flow.think: Squares 23 and 24 are deep sleep and dreaming sleep. Why does the game end with sleep and not with play?

games.title: Muscle Says: contract and relax
games.context: This is a quick game like Simon Says. The caller names a muscle to contract or relax, and players feel it change.

printables.title: 12 caller cards
items: Contract your upper arm: bend your elbow hard.
Relax your upper arm: let it hang.
Contract your tummy: pull it in.
Relax your tummy.
Contract your calf: stand on tiptoe.
Relax your calf: stand flat.
Contract your fist.
Relax your fist.
Contract your thigh: straighten your leg hard.
Relax your thigh.
Contract your cheeks: big smile!
Relax your face.

rules: The caller reads a card. If it begins 'Muscle says', players do it. If not, they stay still.
Players put a hand on the muscle and say 'hard' or 'soft'.
Anyone who moves when the caller did not say 'Muscle says' becomes the next caller.

flow.do: 1. Show how to feel the upper arm muscle while bending the elbow. 2. Explain the rules.
flow.say: When a muscle contracts, it gets short and hard. When it relaxes, it goes soft. Feel your arm.
flow.kid: Put your hand on your upper arm. Bend your elbow hard. Feel it go hard. Now let go. Feel it go soft.
flow.context: This is the first step of Muscle Says. Here you learn to feel a muscle contract and relax.

flow.do: Play through the cards. Mix in a few calls without 'Muscle says'.
flow.say: Muscle says, stand on tiptoe! Is your calf hard or soft?
flow.kid: Listen for 'Muscle says'. Do it, and feel the muscle. Say hard or soft.

check.q: When you stand on tiptoe, what does your calf muscle do?
options: It contracts and gets hard
It relaxes and gets soft
Nothing at all
check.why: To lift your heels, the calf muscle at the back of your lower leg contracts, gets shorter and pulls on your heel bone. When you stand flat again, it relaxes.

flow.do: End by asking about pairs.
flow.say: When you bend your arm, the front muscle contracts. What does the back of your arm do?
flow.kid: Bend your arm. The front muscle is hard. Feel the back of your arm. Is it hard or soft?
flow.think: Muscles can only pull, never push. So how does your arm straighten again?
flow.parent: The muscle at the back of the upper arm relaxes when the arm bends, and contracts to straighten it. Muscles work in pairs, because each one can only pull.

setup.art: A child with a hand on the upper arm, bending the elbow and feeling the muscle bulge.
setup.caption: 1. Feel a muscle contract and relax.

setup.art: A grown-up reading a card while two children stand on tiptoe with hands on their calves.
setup.caption: 2. Do it only if the caller says 'Muscle says'.

experiments.title: The Tired Peg: does rest bring back strength?
experiments.question: If you squeeze a clothes peg again and again without a break, what happens to how many squeezes you can do? And what happens after a short rest?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will squeeze a peg for five rounds of 30 seconds with no break, then rest for two minutes, then do one more round. Will your count stay the same, go up or go down each round? What will happen after the rest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same peg, the same hand and the same two fingers every round. Count only full squeezes, where the two handle ends of the peg touch. The same person times and counts every round. Then a grown-up does the whole test too, because one person's result can be a fluke.

materials.item: a spring clothes peg (a cloth clip), plastic or wooden
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand
paper and a pencil for the table
a helper, to time and count

experiments.safety: Plastic pegs can snap, and a spring can pinch. If the fingers really hurt, with a sharp pain rather than an ache, stop at once.

schedule.what: Guess. Squeeze the peg for five rounds of 30 seconds with no break. Rest two minutes. Do round 6. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw one bar for each round, as tall as the number of squeezes.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the peg. 2. Show a full squeeze: pinch the two handle ends with the thumb and first finger until they touch. 3. Let your child try three squeezes.
flow.say: This is our test machine, a clothes peg. A full squeeze is when the two ends touch. Try three.
flow.kid: Hold the peg between your thumb and first finger. Squeeze until the two ends touch. That is one squeeze. Try three.
flow.parent: Pick a peg with a firm spring. A very soft peg is too easy, and the fingers may not tire. If a peg feels too easy, use two pegs held together.
flow.context: This is the first step of the tired peg test. Here you learn what counts as one full squeeze.

flow.do: 1. Explain the plan: five rounds of 30 seconds with no break, then two minutes of rest, then round 6. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: You will squeeze as fast as you can for 30 seconds, five rounds in a row with no break. Then you rest for two minutes. Then one more round. What do you think will happen to your count? Why?
flow.kid: You will squeeze for five rounds with no break. Then rest. Then one more round. What will happen to your count? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to your count each round, and why?
good: It will go down, because my fingers will get tired.
It will go up, because I will get faster with practice.
After the rest it will go up again, because my fingers will have rested.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Do not say what you expect. Write the guess down so you can compare it with the result.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits with the hand resting on the table. 2. Say 'go' and start the timer. 3. Count every full squeeze out loud, quietly. 4. Say 'stop' at 30 seconds and write the number.
flow.say: Round 1. Ready, go! Squeeze as fast as you can.
flow.kid: Round 1. When your helper says go, squeeze as fast as you can. Stop when they say stop.
flow.parent: Counting under your breath works better than making your child count, so they can put all their effort into squeezing. Most children of 8 manage somewhere between 30 and 70 squeezes in the first round.

flow.do: 1. Go straight on to round 2, with no break. Write the number in 2 or 3 seconds. 2. Do rounds 3, 4 and 5 the same way. 3. After each round, ask how the fingers feel, and write one word.
flow.say: No break! Round 2, go! Keep squeezing as hard as you can. How do your fingers feel now?
flow.kid: No break. Keep going, round after round. Squeeze as fast as you can. How do your fingers feel?
flow.parent: The count usually falls from round to round, and the child says the hand burns, aches or feels slow. If your child slows down on purpose to save strength, remind them to go as fast as they can every round. The test only works if every round is full effort.

flow.do: 1. Your child lays the hand on the table and rests for two minutes. 2. Then do round 6, timed the same way.
flow.say: Now rest for two minutes. Let your hand lie still on the table. Then round 6.
flow.kid: Rest your hand on the table. Wait two minutes. Then do round 6, as fast as you can.

check.q: Riya, a girl in Class 3, did five rounds with no break. Her counts were 50, 44, 39, 35 and 31. After two minutes of rest, what do you think round 6 was?
options: About 25, because she is more tired
About 31, the same as round 5
About 45, because the rest let her fingers recover
check.why: Rest lets the muscle recover. In two minutes, blood brings oxygen and the muscle refills much of its quick fuel, so the count goes up again. Picking 25 means thinking tiredness only builds up. Picking 31 means thinking rest does nothing. Your own round 6 is the real test.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up does the same six rounds while the child times and counts. 2. Compare the pattern of the two sets of numbers.
flow.say: Now it's my turn, and you are the timer and counter. Let's see if my numbers make the same pattern.
flow.kid: Now you are the timer. Your grown-up squeezes. Count their squeezes. Is their pattern like yours?
flow.parent: The grown-up's numbers may be bigger or smaller. What matters is the pattern: falling with no rest, then rising after the rest. If both of you show it, the result is less likely to be a fluke.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a bar chart, one bar per round. 2. Then ask for three sentences: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Draw a bar for each round. Then tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each round. Then say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a muscle gets tired when it works without a break, and rest brings its strength back. What I saw: my count went from 48 to 29 in five rounds, then up to 43 after resting. Why: the muscle used up its fuel, and while I rested my blood helped refill it. Now read the card 'What a working muscle uses up' together.

experiments.context: In this experiment you squeeze a clothes peg again and again, to see how a muscle gets tired and what rest does.

experiments.title: Arm Up, Arm Down: does blood help a muscle keep going?
experiments.question: Do your fingers tire faster when your hand is held up above your head, where less blood reaches it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will squeeze a peg for one minute with your arm held straight up. Later, after a long rest, you will squeeze for one minute with your arm hanging down. Which way will give more squeezes? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same peg, the same hand and the same counter both times. Rest 10 minutes between the two tests, so the fingers start fresh. Do the arm-up test first. That way, if arm-down still wins, it cannot be because you had more practice the second time.

materials.item: the same clothes peg as in the tired peg test
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand
a wall to lean against
paper and a pencil

experiments.safety: Plastic pegs can snap, and a spring can pinch. If the fingers really hurt, with a sharp pain rather than an ache, stop at once. Holding the arm up is tiring for the shoulder too, so rest the back of the arm against a wall.

schedule.what: Squeeze for one minute with the arm up. Rest 10 minutes. Squeeze for one minute with the arm down. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, and draw two bars, one for each arm position.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to hold one hand above the head for one minute, and the other hanging down. 2. Then look at the two hands side by side.
flow.say: Hold one hand up high and let the other hang down, for one minute. Now put them side by side. What do you see?
flow.kid: Hold one hand up high. Let the other hang down. Wait one minute. Now look at both hands together. What is different?

ask.q: Why is the raised hand paler?
good: Blood has to go uphill to reach it, so less gets there.

flow.parent: The raised hand usually looks paler and the hanging hand looks pinker, with fatter veins. Blood has to be pumped uphill to reach a raised hand, so less of it flows there.
flow.context: This is the first step of the arm up, arm down test. Here you see that a raised hand gets less blood.

flow.do: 1. Explain the test. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: First, you squeeze with your arm up for one minute. Then a long rest. Then one minute with your arm down. Which will give more squeezes? Why?
flow.kid: Arm up first. Then rest. Then arm down. Which will give more squeezes? Why do you think so?

flow.do: 1. Your child stands with their back to a wall and raises the squeezing arm straight up, resting it against the wall. 2. Time one minute. Write the count at 30 seconds and at 60 seconds. 3. Ask your child to say 'now' when the ache starts, and write the time.
flow.say: Arm up against the wall. Ready, go! Squeeze as fast as you can. Tell me when it starts to ache.
flow.kid: Lean your back on the wall. Raise your arm straight up. Squeeze fast for one minute. Say 'now' when it starts to ache.
flow.parent: Count quietly. At 30 seconds, note the count without stopping. Most children feel the ache sooner with the arm up.

flow.do: 1. Rest for 10 minutes. Read the Pongal story, or play a game. 2. Then do one minute with the arm hanging down at the side, timed and counted the same way.
flow.say: Now a long rest, so your fingers start fresh. Then the same test with your arm hanging down.
flow.kid: Rest for 10 minutes. Then do it again with your arm hanging down. Squeeze fast for one minute. Say 'now' when it aches.

flow.do: 1. Compare the totals and the ache times. 2. Ask for what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Which way gave more squeezes? When did the ache start each time? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Which way gave more squeezes? Which started aching sooner? Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: Why do fingers usually tire faster when the arm is held up?
options: The peg gets heavier when it is held up
Less blood reaches the hand, so less oxygen arrives to refill the muscle
Fingers are always weaker in the morning
check.why: Blood has to be pumped uphill to a raised hand, so less flows there. Less blood means less oxygen to help the muscle refill its fuel, and slower removal of waste. Picking 'the peg gets heavier' means thinking the load changed. It did not: the same peg was used both times.

flow.parent: Usually the arm-down count is higher and the ache comes later. If your child's results are the other way round, ask what might have been different, such as tired fingers from earlier or counting mistakes. Try again another day.

experiments.context: In this experiment you squeeze a peg with your arm held up and then hanging down, to see whether blood flow changes how fast a muscle tires.

experiments.title: Taller in the Morning? A bedtime and wake-up measure
experiments.question: Is your height the same at bedtime and just after you wake up?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will you be taller, shorter or the same height in the morning as at bedtime? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Measure at the same spot on the same wall, barefoot, standing the same way, with the same book and the same tape. Measure three times each time, because one mark can be a little off. In the morning, measure as soon as you get up, before walking about much.

materials.item: a measuring tape, a tailor's inch tape, or a metre scale
a hardback book or a small wooden board
a pencil, and a strip of paper taped to the wall if you cannot mark the wall

experiments.safety: None, but a grown-up should hold the book, so it does not slip onto your child's face.

schedule.what: At bedtime: measure your height three times against the wall and write the numbers.
As soon as you wake up: measure three times again in the same way. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Work out how many millimetres taller or shorter you were in the morning.

flow.do: 1. At bedtime, ask the question. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: Do you think you are the same height at bedtime as in the morning? Why?
flow.kid: Are you the same height at night and in the morning? Guess. Why do you think so?
flow.context: This is the first step of the taller in the morning test. Here you make your guess at bedtime.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands barefoot with heels, bottom and shoulders touching the wall, looking straight ahead. 2. Lay the book flat on the head, pressed against the wall. 3. Draw a thin line under the book. 4. Step away and measure from the floor to the line. 5. Do it three times.
flow.say: Heels, bottom and shoulders on the wall. Look straight ahead. I'll put the book on your head and draw a line.
flow.kid: Stand with your heels, bottom and shoulders on the wall. Look straight ahead. Stand still while your grown-up marks the wall.
flow.parent: Press the book down gently so it rests on the top of the head, not on hair. Use the middle of the three numbers. A tailor's tape is fine. Read it to the nearest millimetre, the small lines between the centimetres.

flow.do: 1. In the morning, measure as soon as your child gets out of bed, in the same way, three times. 2. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Good morning! Before anything else, let's measure you, the same way as last night.
flow.kid: Good morning! Go straight to the wall. Stand the same way as last night. Your grown-up measures you three times.
flow.wait: Do this step the next morning, as soon as your child wakes up.
flow.parent: Most people are taller in the morning, often by about half a centimetre to one centimetre. If the difference is only 1 or 2 millimetres, it could be a measuring mistake. Measure a grown-up too: adults often show a bigger change.

flow.do: 1. Work out the difference. 2. Ask for what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: How much taller or shorter were you this morning? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Take away the night number from the morning number. That is the difference. What do you think made it?

check.q: Why are most people a little taller in the morning?
options: Children grow a whole centimetre every night
The soft discs in the backbone soak up water while you lie down, and get squashed again during the day
Feet get flatter in the morning
check.why: All day, standing and sitting squeeze some water out of the discs between the bones of your backbone. Lying down at night takes the weight off, and they soak it back up. Children do grow, but much more slowly: about 5 or 6 centimetres in a whole year.

experiments.context: In this experiment you measure your height at bedtime and as soon as you wake up, to see what a night of lying down does to your backbone.

activities.title: The Heavy Bottle: why does a light thing get heavy?

materials.item: a one-litre plastic water bottle, full and with the cap on
a phone timer or a clock

activities.safety: Use a plastic bottle, not glass. Stop as soon as the arm drops.

schedule.what: Hold a full bottle out at shoulder height for as long as you can. Notice what the arm does. Rest and try again.

activities.record: Write how many seconds you held the bottle the first time and the second time.
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You hold a bottle of water out to the side until your arm cannot hold it any more.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the full bottle in one hand, arm straight out to the side at shoulder height. 2. Start the timer. 3. Stop when the arm drops below the shoulder.
flow.say: Hold the bottle straight out to the side, as long as you can. Tell me how it feels as you go.
flow.kid: Hold the bottle out to the side. Keep your arm straight. Hold it as long as you can. How does it feel?
flow.parent: Most children hold it for somewhere between 30 seconds and 2 minutes. The arm starts to shake and burn before it drops. Write down the time.
flow.context: This is the first step of the heavy bottle activity. Here you hold a bottle out until your arm drops.

flow.do: Ask the question, and wait for a guess with a reason.
flow.say: The bottle weighed the same all the time. So why did it feel heavier and heavier?
flow.kid: The bottle did not get heavier. So why did it feel heavier? What do you think?

ask.q: Why did the bottle feel heavier and heavier?
good: The muscles were working without a rest.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Let your child guess. The unit answers this in the peg test.

flow.do: 1. Rest the arm for one minute. 2. Try again, timing it. 3. Compare the two times.
flow.say: Rest your arm for one minute. Then try again. Will you last as long as the first time?
flow.kid: Rest for one minute. Then hold the bottle out again. Did you last as long?
flow.think: After one minute of rest, some strength came back, but maybe not all of it. Where did it come back from?

setup.caption: 1. Hold a full bottle straight out to the side.

setup.art: The child's arm shaking and dropping, the bottle lower than the shoulder.
setup.caption: 2. Stop when your arm drops. Rest, then try again.

activities.title: Three Poses and a Bee Breath: a short yoga session

materials.item: a yoga mat, a folded bedsheet or a durrie on the floor

activities.safety: Move slowly and stop if anything hurts. Never bounce in a stretch.

schedule.what: Mountain pose, tree pose, cobra pose, then the bee breath, then child's pose to rest.

activities.record: Write how many seconds you held tree pose on each leg, and draw yourself in your favourite pose.
activities.context: In this activity you try three yoga poses and a yoga breath, and notice which muscles work in each one.

flow.do: 1. Stand tall with feet together and arms by the sides. 2. Breathe slowly five times. This is mountain pose, tadasana.
flow.say: This is mountain pose. Stand tall like a mountain. Feel your feet pressing into the floor.
flow.kid: Stand tall, feet together, arms by your sides. Breathe slowly five times. This is mountain pose.
flow.context: This is the first step of a short yoga session. Here you stand in mountain pose.

flow.do: 1. Shift the weight onto one foot. 2. Place the other foot on the inside of the calf or thigh, never on the knee. 3. Join the hands. 4. Time how long your child stays up, to a limit of 60 seconds. 5. Swap legs.
flow.say: Now tree pose, vrikshasana. Look at one spot on the wall to help you balance. I'll time you.
flow.kid: Stand on one leg. Put your other foot on the inside of your leg, not on the knee. Look at one spot. How long can you stay?
flow.parent: Tiny wobbles are normal. The muscles in the standing foot and leg are working and relaxing all the time to keep the body steady. Ask your child to feel the ankle.

flow.do: 1. Lie on the tummy with hands under the shoulders. 2. Press gently and lift the head and chest, keeping the hips down. 3. Hold for three breaths. Lower slowly.
flow.say: This is cobra pose, bhujangasana. Lift your chest slowly, like a cobra lifting their head. Keep your hips on the floor.
flow.kid: Lie on your tummy. Hands under your shoulders. Lift your head and chest slowly. Breathe three times. Come down slowly.
flow.parent: Keep the elbows a little bent. The pose should feel like a gentle stretch at the front of the body, never a pinch in the back.

flow.do: 1. Sit cross-legged and close the eyes. 2. Breathe in through the nose. 3. Breathe out slowly while humming, like a bee, with the mouth closed. 4. Do it five times. This is bhramari, the bee breath.
flow.say: Breathe in. Now breathe out slowly, humming like a bee, with your mouth closed. Can you feel your head buzz?
flow.kid: Sit and close your eyes. Breathe in through your nose. Breathe out and hum like a bee. Feel the buzz. Do it five times.

flow.do: 1. Kneel, sit back on the heels and bend forward until the forehead rests on the floor. 2. Rest the arms by the sides. 3. Stay for six slow breaths. This is child's pose, balasana.
flow.say: Now child's pose. Rest your forehead on the floor. Let every muscle go soft.
flow.kid: Kneel and sit back on your heels. Bend forward. Rest your forehead on the floor. Breathe slowly six times.

check.q: In tree pose, why does your standing ankle keep wobbling a little?
options: Because yoga is too hard for children
Because the muscles in your leg are making tiny changes all the time to keep you balanced
Because the floor is moving
check.why: Staying balanced is not one big push. The muscles in your foot and leg keep making tiny corrections, contracting and relaxing, to keep your weight over your foot. Practice makes the corrections quicker and smaller.

activities.title: My Sleep Diary and 24-Hour Circle

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a plate and paper, to draw a big circle
coloured pencils

schedule.what: Make the diary table. Write tonight's bedtime.
Write the wake-up time, the hours slept, and how you feel. Write tonight's bedtime.
The same as day 2.
The same as day 2.
The same as day 2.
The same as day 2.
Fill in the last row. Draw a 24-hour circle of one day. Look for a pattern.

activities.record: A table with these columns: date, bedtime, wake-up time, hours slept, how I felt (great, fine or tired), how long I played or exercised.
activities.context: In this 7-day activity you keep a diary of your sleep, and then draw one whole day as a circle of 24 hours.

flow.do: 1. Draw the diary table in the notebook. 2. Fill in tonight's bedtime: the time the lights go off.
flow.say: For one week, we'll write down when you sleep and wake, and how you feel. Then we'll look for a pattern.
flow.kid: Draw a table with six columns. Write the date and your bedtime tonight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the sleep diary. Here you make the table.

flow.do: 1. Each morning, write the wake-up time. 2. Count the hours slept. 3. Write how your child feels: great, fine or tired.
flow.say: What time did you wake up? Let's count how many hours you slept. How do you feel this morning?
flow.kid: Write the time you woke up. Count the hours from bedtime. How do you feel? Write great, fine or tired.
flow.wait: Do this every morning for 6 days.
flow.parent: Counting hours across midnight is good time practice. From 9 at night to 6 in the morning is 9 hours: 3 hours to midnight and 6 more after it.

flow.do: 1. On day 7, draw round a plate to make a big circle. 2. Divide it into 24 slices, one for each hour. 3. Colour the hours of sleep, school or study, play and meals in different colours.
flow.say: Let's draw one day as a circle. Each slice is one hour. Which colour takes up the most room?
flow.kid: Draw a big circle. Cut it into 24 slices, one for each hour. Colour your sleep hours blue. Colour your play hours green.
flow.parent: To make 24 slices, draw a cross to make 4 quarters, then split each quarter into 3, then split each of those in half.

flow.do: Look across the week together and ask about the pattern.
flow.say: On the mornings you felt great, how many hours had you slept? On the tired mornings?
flow.kid: Look at your table. On great mornings, how long did you sleep? On tired mornings?

check.q: How many hours of sleep does a child of 8 need each night?
options: About 5 to 6 hours
About 9 to 12 hours
About 14 to 16 hours
check.why: Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours a night. Grown-ups need about 7 to 9. Babies need even more than children. If your diary shows fewer than 9 hours on most nights, try an earlier bedtime for a week and see how you feel.

activities.title: Stamina, Strength or Stretch? Sort and try

materials.item: 12 small paper slips and a pencil
three bowls or three sheets of paper as labels

activities.safety: Do the moves on a clear floor, away from furniture. No jumping if the neighbours below will be disturbed: march on the spot instead.

schedule.what: Write 12 activities on slips. Sort them into stamina, strength and stretch. Try one of each for one minute.

activities.record: Write your three groups. Circle the activities you do in a normal week.
activities.context: In this activity you sort everyday activities into three kinds of exercise, and try one of each.

flow.do: 1. Write one activity on each slip. Use skipping, climbing stairs, kho-kho, swimming, cycling and carrying a bucket of water. Add wall push-ups, yoga, touching your toes, kabaddi, Bharatanatyam and sweeping the floor. 2. Label three bowls: stamina, strength and stretch.
flow.say: Stamina means keeping going for a long time. Strength means pushing or pulling hard. Stretch means bending far. Let's sort these.
flow.kid: Read each slip. Is it mostly stamina, strength or stretch? Put it in a bowl.
flow.context: This is the first step of the exercise sort. Here you write the slips and label the bowls.

flow.do: Your child sorts the slips and explains each choice.
flow.say: Why did you put kabaddi there? Could it go in more than one bowl?
flow.kid: Sort all 12 slips. Some could go in two bowls. Which ones?

ask.q: Which activities use more than one kind?
good: Kabaddi uses stamina, strength and stretch.
Bharatanatyam needs stamina, strength and flexibility.

flow.parent: There is no single right answer for many slips. A good answer explains what the body does: kabaddi needs running for a long time, holding and pulling, and bending low.

flow.do: 1. Do one minute of each: marching fast on the spot for stamina, wall push-ups for strength, and a slow toe-touch for stretch. 2. After each, ask what the body felt.
flow.say: One minute of each. After each one, tell me what you felt. Was it your breath, your muscles, or a stretch?
flow.kid: March fast on the spot for one minute. Then do wall push-ups for one minute. Then touch your toes slowly. What did each one feel like?
flow.think: Which kind of exercise do you do the least? How could you add some to your week?

projects.title: My Ten-Day Yoga Log: does practice make me steadier?

materials.item: a yoga mat, a folded bedsheet or a durrie
a phone timer
a ruler or measuring tape
a notebook

projects.safety: Move slowly, and stop if anything hurts. Never bounce in a stretch.

schedule.what: Day 1 test: time tree pose on each leg, up to 60 seconds. Do the sit and reach test. Write the numbers.
Practise tree pose and the toe-touch stretch for 5 minutes.
Practise for 5 minutes.
Practise for 5 minutes.
Practise for 5 minutes, then test again and write the numbers.
Practise for 5 minutes.
Practise for 5 minutes.
Practise for 5 minutes.
Practise for 5 minutes.
Final test. Draw a chart of your tree pose times and reach on days 1, 5 and 10.

projects.record: A table with columns: day, tree pose on the left leg (seconds), tree pose on the right leg (seconds), sit and reach (cm).
projects.context: In this 10-day project you practise yoga for five minutes a day, and test whether your balance and stretch improve.

flow.do: 1. Time tree pose on each leg, up to 60 seconds. Stop the timer when the raised foot touches the floor. 2. Write both times.
flow.say: Today is test day. Let's see how long you can stand in tree pose on each leg.
flow.kid: Stand in tree pose on your left leg. Your grown-up times you. Then the right leg. Write both numbers.
flow.context: This is the first step of the ten-day yoga log. Here you test your balance on day 1.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits on the floor with legs straight, feet flat against a wall. 2. Lay a ruler on the floor between the legs, pointing at the wall. 3. Your child reaches forward slowly with both hands, and holds for 2 seconds. 4. Measure how far the fingertips are from the wall.
flow.say: Now the sit and reach test. Reach forward slowly. Don't bounce. Hold it while I measure.
flow.kid: Sit with your feet flat on the wall. Reach slowly towards the wall. Hold still. How far are your fingers from the wall?
flow.parent: If the fingertips reach past the toes and touch the wall, write the reach as 0, and measure how far up the wall they go next time. The same reach done fast or with a bounce is not fair.

flow.do: Every day from day 2, your child practises for 5 minutes. First, tree pose on each leg. Then the toe-touch stretch, held for three slow breaths, three times.
flow.say: Five minutes of practice. Tree pose on each leg, then three slow toe-touch stretches.
flow.kid: Practise tree pose on each leg. Then reach for your toes slowly. Hold for three breaths. Do it three times.
flow.wait: Practise every day for days 2 to 9, and test again on day 5 and day 10.

flow.do: 1. On day 10, test again. 2. Draw a bar chart of tree pose times on days 1, 5 and 10. 3. Ask for what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Did your times change? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Draw a bar for day 1, day 5 and day 10. Did you get steadier? Why do you think so?

check.q: Lakshmi's tree pose time went from 12 seconds on day 1 to 40 seconds on day 10. What is the best explanation?
options: Her leg grew longer
Her body and brain got better at the tiny corrections that keep her balanced
The floor got flatter
check.why: Practice trains the muscles and the brain together. The tiny corrections that keep you balanced become quicker and smaller. Ten days is too short for legs to grow much, and the floor stayed the same.

flow.parent: Most children improve their tree pose time within ten days. The reach may change only a little. Both are real results. If nothing changed, ask your child what might help, such as practising at the same time every day.

challenges.title: The Monsoon Workout: exercise in a small flat
challenges.problem: It has rained for a week, and nobody can go out to play. Design a 10-minute workout for a small flat that builds stamina, strength and flexibility, without disturbing the neighbours downstairs.
constraints: It must fit in a space the size of a single bed.
No jumping or stamping, because the neighbours below will hear.
It must include at least one stamina move, one strength move and one stretch.
It must last 10 minutes, with short rests.
materials: a mat or a folded bedsheet
a stair, if your building has one
general: March fast on the spot, or dance on the spot, for stamina.
Wall push-ups, or sitting against a wall as if on a chair, for strength.
Cobra pose and a toe-touch stretch for flexibility.
Work for one minute, then rest for 30 seconds, then the next move.
creative: Make a dice where each number is a move, and roll for the order.
Climb the building stairs slowly, one floor at a time, if your building has stairs.
Make it a dance to your favourite song, with each verse a different kind of move.
challenges.your_turn: Now plan your own monsoon workout. Write the moves and the rest times on a card. Do it with your family, and time it. Did it work your breath, your muscles and your stretch?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You plan a workout for a rainy day in a small flat.

flow.do: Read the problem and the rules together.
flow.say: It's been raining for a week. Plan a 10-minute workout for our flat, with no jumping.
flow.kid: Rain all week! Plan a 10-minute workout in a small space. No jumping. Include stamina, strength and stretch.
flow.context: This is the first step of the monsoon workout challenge. Here you read the problem.

flow.kid: Write your moves. How long is each one? Put in rests. Why do you need them?

ask.q: Why put rests between the moves?
good: So the muscles can recover, like in the peg test.
So the blood can refill the muscles before the next move.

flow.do: Do the workout together, timed. Then talk about what to change.
flow.say: Let's do it! Afterwards, tell me what worked and what you would change.
flow.kid: Do your workout with your family. Time it. What would you change next time?

challenges.title: The Sleep Den: help someone fall asleep in a noisy city
challenges.problem: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, lives beside a busy road in Hyderabad. A street light shines into her room, autos honk late at night, and her room gets hot. She keeps waking up. Design changes to her room and her bedtime that would help her sleep through the night.
constraints: You may only use things that most homes have, or that are cheap to buy.
The family cannot move house or change rooms.
The plan must deal with light, noise and heat.
materials: a shoebox, to make a model room
dark cloth, cotton wool, foil and cardboard for the model
general: Hang a dark curtain or a thick bedsheet over the window to block the street light.
Use a fan, which also covers small noises with a steady hum.
Stop screens an hour before bed, because bright screens make it harder to feel sleepy.
Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day.
creative: Put the head of the bed on the wall furthest from the road.
Fold a soft cloth into an eye mask.
Make a bedtime routine card with pictures: bath, brush, story, lights out.
Open the window on the far side of the flat in the evening to let cooler air through.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own sleep den for Kavya. Build it as a model in a shoebox, or draw it. Then write a bedtime routine for her with five steps.

flow.kid: Make Kavya's room in a shoebox, or draw it. Fix the light. Fix the noise. Fix the heat.

flow.parent: Bright light in the evening, especially from screens, delays the body's sleep signal, a hormone called melatonin. A dark, cool, quiet room and a steady bedtime help most children sleep better.
