quiz.p: Meena, a girl in Class 3, squeezes a clothes peg for five rounds of 30 seconds with no break. What usually happens to her count?
quiz.why: With no break, her finger muscles use up their quick fuel faster than her blood can help refill it, so each round she manages fewer squeezes. Picking 'goes up' means thinking practice wins over tiredness in a few minutes.

quiz.p: After the five rounds, Meena rests her hand for two minutes. What happens to her next count?
quiz.why: During the rest, blood brings oxygen and the muscle refills much of its fuel. Picking 'falls even lower' means thinking rest does nothing.

quiz.p: What does blood bring to a working muscle?
quiz.why: Blood carries oxygen from the lungs and food from the gut. The muscle uses them to refill its fuel. Blood also carries waste away.

quiz.p: Why is it a fair test to use the same peg and the same hand in every round?
opts: So only the rest changes, and nothing else
quiz.why: In a fair test you change only one thing. If you used a softer peg in one round, you would not know whether the peg or the rest changed the count.

quiz.p: Which of these is mainly a stamina exercise?
quiz.why: Stamina means keeping going for a long time, which works the heart and lungs. Touching the toes is a stretch. Carrying a heavy bucket is mostly strength.

quiz.p: What is a yoga pose called?
quiz.why: Asana is the Sanskrit word for a yoga pose. A raga is a pattern of notes in music. A kolam is a pattern drawn on the floor.

quiz.p: Which yoga practice is about breathing slowly in a set way?
quiz.why: Pranayama is the breathing part of yoga. Tree pose and child's pose are poses, called asanas.

quiz.p: How many hours of sleep does a child of 8 need each night?
quiz.why: Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours. Six hours is too little for a child. Fifteen hours is closer to what a baby sleeps.

quiz.p: What does the brain do during dreaming sleep?
opts: It is nearly as busy as when you are awake
quiz.why: Recordings of the brain's signals show it is very active in dreaming sleep. For a long time people thought the brain switched off at night. That was shown wrong in 1953.

quiz.p: Eugene Aserinsky, a scientist, recorded his son Armond sleeping. What did he see several times a night?
opts: Armond's eyes darting about under his closed eyelids
quiz.why: Aserinsky saw bursts of rapid eye movement, with busy brain signals. People woken at those times usually said they had been dreaming. This was dreaming sleep, or REM sleep.

quiz.p: Why are most people a little taller in the morning than at bedtime?
opts: The discs in their backbone fill up with water while they lie down
quiz.why: Standing and sitting squeeze water out of the soft discs between the bones of the backbone. Lying down lets them soak it back. Children grow only about 5 or 6 centimetres in a whole year.

quiz.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 3, has a test tomorrow. Which plan will help his body and brain most?
opts: Study late until midnight, then wake up at 6
Study, play outside, and go to bed on time for 10 hours of sleep
Skip dinner and study all evening
quiz.why: Sleep helps the brain store what was learned, and play gives the body exercise. Studying until midnight leaves only 6 hours of sleep, far less than a child needs.

items.p: When does a muscle get tired fastest?
opts: When it works hard without any rest
When it works a little and then rests
items.why: Working hard without rest uses up the muscle's quick fuel faster than blood can help refill it.
items.art: A hand squeezing a peg with a timer, and a resting hand beside it.

items.p: Which word means a muscle getting shorter and pulling?
items.why: A muscle contracts to pull. When it stops pulling and goes soft, it relaxes.

items.p: Why do you breathe faster when you run?
opts: To take in more oxygen for your working muscles
items.why: Working muscles need more oxygen, so you breathe faster, and your heart pumps faster to carry it to them.

items.p: Which of these is a flexibility exercise?
items.why: Cobra pose bends the back gently and stretches the front of the body. Running builds stamina, and carrying builds strength.

items.p: Which helps a child sleep well?
opts: A bright phone screen in bed
A big, sugary drink at bedtime
items.why: Darkness, quiet and coolness help the body feel sleepy. Bright screens delay the body's sleep signal.

items.p: The brain switches off completely while you sleep.
items.why: False. The brain stays busy, especially in dreaming sleep, when it is nearly as active as when you are awake.

items.p: Astronauts must exercise every day in space to keep their bones and muscles strong.
items.why: True. In space, bones and muscles carry no weight, so they get weaker unless astronauts exercise for about two hours a day.

items.p: The breathing part of yoga is called ____.
items.why: Pranayama means slow breathing in a set way, such as the bee breath.

items.p: Most vivid dreams happen in ____ sleep, also called REM sleep.
items.why: REM stands for rapid eye movement, because the eyes dart about in this part of sleep.

items.p: Match each exercise to the kind it mostly builds.
items.why: Stamina keeps you going, strength pushes and pulls hard, flexibility bends far, and balance keeps you steady.

items.p: Sort these into what helps your body rest and what makes it work.
items: sleeping
Rest
child's pose
Rest
slow breathing
Rest
kabaddi
Work
climbing stairs
Work
skipping
Work
items.why: Rest gives the body time to refill and repair. Work uses up its fuel.

items.p: Put the steps of the tired peg test in order.
items: Rest for two minutes
Squeeze for five rounds with no break
Guess what will happen, and why
Do one more round
a: Guess what will happen, and why
Squeeze for five rounds with no break
items.why: First guess, then tire the muscle, then rest, then test again to see what rest did.

items.p: In the tired peg test, what happened to your count after two minutes of rest? Say why.
items.a: My count went up again after the rest. While I rested, my blood brought oxygen, and the muscle refilled its fuel and got rid of waste.
items.why: A strong answer gives the numbers from the test and says what the blood did during the rest.

items.p: Write two things your body does while you sleep.
items.a: It releases growth hormone in deep sleep, which helps me grow and repair. My brain dreams and sorts what I learned. The discs in my back fill up with water.
items.why: Any two true things show that sleep is a busy time, not doing nothing.

items.p: Draw yourself in tree pose. Mark the leg muscles that are working hardest.
items.a: A child standing on one leg, with the standing leg's calf, thigh and ankle marked.
items.why: The standing leg does all the work, making tiny corrections to keep you balanced.
items.art: A blank box with a floor line.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Class 3, squeezes a peg for one minute with her arm up, and later with her arm down. Which way do her fingers usually tire faster?
items.why: With the arm up, blood has to be pumped uphill, so less reaches the hand. Less oxygen arrives to help the muscle refill.

items.p: In the arm up, arm down test, why do the arm-up round first?
opts: So that if arm-down still wins, it cannot be because of extra practice
Because arms are stronger in the morning
It does not matter at all
items.why: The second try often goes better because you have practised. Doing arm-up first puts that extra practice on the arm-down side, so a win for arm-down must come from something else, such as blood flow.

items.p: Lactic acid is cleared from muscles within about an hour. So what causes the ache the next day after hard exercise?
opts: Tiny injuries in the muscle, which heal and make it stronger
Lactic acid still sitting in the muscle
items.why: The next-day ache comes from tiny injuries that heal over a few days. The muscle rebuilds a little stronger.

items.p: Why does a child need more sleep than a grown-up?
opts: Children are growing, and much growth hormone is released in deep sleep
items.why: A growing body uses deep sleep to release growth hormone. Children also learn a great deal each day, and sleep helps store it.

items.p: A muscle can only pull, never push.
items.why: True. That is why muscles work in pairs: one pulls to bend your arm, and another pulls to straighten it.

items.p: The soft pads between the bones of your backbone are called ____.
items.why: Discs hold water like a sponge. They get slightly squashed during the day and fill up at night.

items.p: Sort these by what happens during sleep and what does not.
items: growth hormone is released
Happens in sleep
the eyes dart about at times
Happens in sleep
the brain sorts memories
Happens in sleep
the heart stops
Does not happen in sleep
the brain switches off
Does not happen in sleep
items.why: The heart keeps beating and the brain stays busy all night.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Skipping, cycling, swimming, sleeping.
items.why: Skipping, cycling and swimming are stamina exercises. Sleeping is rest.

items.p: Put the parts of a night in order for a child who falls asleep at 9 p.m.
items: dreaming sleep, with eyes darting
light sleep, just after lights out
waking up in the morning
deep sleep, with slow breathing
a: light sleep, just after lights out
items.why: Each sleep cycle goes from light sleep to deep sleep, then dreaming sleep. The cycle repeats several times before morning.

items.p: Your hand looked paler after you held it up for one minute. What does that tell you about blood? How does it explain the arm-up peg result?
items.a: Less blood was in the raised hand, because it had to be pumped uphill. With less blood, less oxygen reached the finger muscles, so they could not refill their fuel as fast, and tired sooner.
items.why: A strong answer links the colour to blood, and the blood to the muscle's fuel.

items.p: Your grown-up's peg counts were bigger than yours, but both sets fell and then rose after rest. Why does the pattern matter more than the size of the numbers?
items.a: The question was about what rest does. Both of us showed counts falling with no rest and rising after it. Bigger hands just give bigger numbers. The same pattern in two people makes the result less likely to be a fluke.
items.why: A strong answer says that the test compared rounds within one person, not people with each other.

items.p: Many people say 'Exercise makes you tired, so if you exercise less you will have more energy.' Is that right? Use what you learned to explain.
items.a: Not over weeks. Exercise tires you for a short time, but rest refills the muscles. Over weeks, regular exercise makes the heart and muscles stronger, so everyday things feel easier and you have more energy.
items.why: A strong answer separates the short tiredness right after exercise from what regular exercise does over weeks.

items.p: Nandini, a girl in Class 4, and her cousin Vikram are arguing about the tired peg test.

views.says: My fingers slowed down because the muscle ran out of fuel. My count fell, so the muscle was getting empty.
Your brain slowed you down to protect your fingers. You could have kept going if you had really tried.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use your own peg results. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence. For Nandini: the counts fell even though I tried my hardest, and the arm-up test tired faster when less blood came, which points to fuel in the muscle. For Vikram: some runners can sprint at the finish, so the brain may hold some strength back. Many scientists think both happen.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. A good answer uses evidence and is fair to the other side.

items.p: Draw a bar chart of these made-up peg counts: round 1, 50. Round 2, 42. Round 3, 37. Round 4, 33. Round 5 after a two-minute rest, 46.
items.a: Five bars, falling from 50 to 33, then a tall bar of 46 for the round after rest.
items.why: The chart shows the falling counts without rest and the jump back after rest.
items.art: Empty axes labelled round and squeezes, with marks every 10.

items.p: Label the parts of a night's sleep on the circle: light sleep, deep sleep, dreaming sleep.
items.a: Light sleep first, then deep sleep, then dreaming sleep, before the cycle begins again.
items.why: A night is made of several of these cycles.
items.art: A circle divided into three unlabelled parts, with an arrow showing the direction of the cycle.

items.p: A cricket fast bowler bowls six balls in an over, then fields for a few minutes before the next over. Why does the rest between overs help?
opts: It gives the blood time to help refill the leg and arm muscles
It lets the ball cool down
It has nothing to do with the bowler's muscles
items.why: Short rests let working muscles refill their quick fuel and clear waste, so the next over can be fast again.

items.p: On the space station, astronauts strap themselves to a treadmill with belts. Why?
opts: So their bones get jolts and carry weight, as they do on Earth
So they do not float into the walls while sleeping
So the treadmill does not break
items.why: Bones get stronger when they carry weight and get jolted. In space nothing presses down, so belts pull the astronaut onto the treadmill.

items.p: Why can a tired runner often sprint the last 100 metres of a race?
opts: The muscles still had some fuel left, and the brain lets more be used near the finish
The track is shorter at the end
items.why: This is one reason some scientists think the brain holds back some strength to keep the body safe, and lets more out near the finish.

items.p: A dolphin must swim up to breathe, even at night. How does a dolphin sleep?
opts: With one half of their brain at a time
items.why: Dolphins rest one half of their brain while the other half stays awake enough to swim and breathe.

items.p: Sleeping late on Sunday fully makes up for a whole week of going to bed too late.
items.why: False. A long sleep helps, but studies find it does not undo all the effects of a week of short nights. A steady bedtime works better.

items.p: In 1927, Yellapragada Subbarow and Cyrus Fiske found a quick fuel in muscle called ____.
items.why: Phosphocreatine is the store a muscle uses in short, hard bursts, and refills during rest.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? A heart between beats, a muscle after the peg test, a sleeping child, a running child.
opts: A muscle after the peg test
items.why: The first three are resting and refilling. The running child is using up fuel.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shortest rest to the longest.
items: a night's sleep
the pause between two heartbeats
two minutes of rest after the peg test
a: two minutes of rest after the peg test
items.why: A heart rests for less than a second between beats. A muscle can recover in minutes. A night's sleep lasts many hours.

items.p: Many people think resting is wasted time. Using the peg test and what you learned about sleep, explain whether you agree.
items.a: I disagree. In the peg test my count rose after two minutes of rest, because my blood helped refill the muscle. In sleep, growth hormone is released, my brain sorts memories, and the discs in my back fill up. Rest is when the body refills, repairs and grows.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the test and from sleep, not only opinion.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether children do better at the tree pose after a long night's sleep than after a short one. What would you change, and what would you keep the same?
items.a: Change only the hours of sleep: one night of about 10 hours and one night of about 8. Keep the same child, the same time of the morning, the same floor and the same timer. Do the test on several mornings of each kind, because one morning can be a fluke.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, and repeats the test.

items.p: Eugene Aserinsky first thought the machine was broken when the lines went wild. Why was it important that he tested again and again, and with other sleepers?
items.a: If it was a broken machine, it would go wild at random times. It happened at regular times each night, and in other people too, so it was real. Testing again ruled out a fault.
items.why: A strong answer says how repeating a test separates a real finding from a mistake.

items.p: Your sleep diary shows that on the three mornings you felt tired, you had slept fewer than 9 hours. Does this prove short sleep made you tired? What else could explain it?
items.a: It does not fully prove it. Something else might have caused both, such as being ill or a late, exciting day. To be surer, I could keep the diary for longer, or try going to bed earlier for a week and see if I feel better.
items.why: A strong answer sees that two things happening together does not always mean one caused the other.

items.p: Your heart rests between every beat, and you rest every night. Name two other things in nature that work and rest in turns.
items.a: A tamarind tree folds their leaves at night and opens them in the day. The sea comes in and goes out with the tides. Birds sleep at night and fly in the day.
items.why: Any two true examples of a rhythm of activity and rest are good.

items.p: Pooja, a girl in Class 5, wants to stay up late to practise the veena for a concert. Her aunt Shalini thinks she should go to bed. Her friend Ritu says she should do both, a little.

views.says: More practice means I will play better. Every hour counts.
Sleep helps your brain store what you practised. A tired player makes more mistakes.
Practise slowly for a short time, then sleep. You need both.

open_questions.q: Why do animals need to sleep at all?
open_questions.why_open: Sleep may help repair the body, store memories and clean the brain, but nobody knows which of these is the main reason, or whether there is one.
Some scientists think dreams help the brain sort memories and feelings. Others think they are a side effect of a busy brain. Nobody can test it fully yet.

open_questions.q: How much of tiredness comes from the muscle, and how much from the brain?
open_questions.why_open: Both seem to play a part, and scientists still argue about how much each matters.
Seeing someone yawn makes many people yawn too, and some animals do it. Scientists have several ideas about why, and none is agreed.

maths.problem: In the tired peg test, Meera's counts were 48, 41, 36, 32 and 29 in five rounds with no break. How many fewer squeezes did she do in round 5 than in round 1?
maths.explain: 48 take away 29 is 19. Count up from 29: 1 more makes 30, then 18 more makes 48. 1 + 18 = 19.
maths.context: This is about the tired peg test, where you squeeze a clothes peg for 30 seconds, again and again, with no break.
maths.why_maths: Taking away shows how much strength the muscle lost, as a single number.

maths.problem: Look at how much Meera's count fell each round: 48 to 41, 41 to 36, 36 to 32, 32 to 29. Is the fall getting bigger or smaller? Guess what round 6 would be without a rest.
maths.answer: The fall gets smaller each round: 7, then 5, then 4, then 3. Round 6 would probably be about 26 or 27.
maths.explain: 48 − 41 = 7. 41 − 36 = 5. 36 − 32 = 4. 32 − 29 = 3. The drops shrink, so the next drop might be about 2 or 3. 29 − 3 = 26.
maths.context: This is about the tired peg test, where you squeeze a peg for 30 seconds, again and again, with no break.
maths.why_maths: Finding the pattern in the drops lets you predict what would happen next, before you test it.

maths.problem: After resting for two minutes, Meera's count went from 29 back up to 43. Her first round was 48. Did the rest bring back all of her strength?
maths.answer: Not all of it. She got back 14 of the 19 squeezes she had lost.
maths.explain: She lost 48 − 29 = 19 squeezes. The rest brought her up 43 − 29 = 14. 19 − 14 = 5, so she was still 5 short of round 1. A longer rest would probably bring back the rest.
maths.context: This is about the tired peg test. After five rounds with no break, you rest for two minutes and squeeze again.
maths.why_maths: Comparing what was lost with what came back tells you how much a short rest helps.

maths.problem: Kavya goes to sleep at 9 at night and wakes up at 6:30 in the morning. How long did she sleep? Is it enough for a child of 8?
maths.answer: 9 and a half hours. Yes, it is within the 9 to 12 hours a child of 8 needs.
maths.explain: From 9 at night to midnight is 3 hours. From midnight to 6 in the morning is 6 hours. Then 30 more minutes to 6:30. 3 + 6 = 9 hours, plus half an hour.
maths.context: This is about the sleep diary, where you write when you go to bed and when you wake up.
maths.why_maths: Working out how long you slept, across midnight, is the only way to check it against what your body needs.

maths.problem: In a 24-hour day, a child sleeps for 10 hours. How many hours are left for everything else?
maths.explain: 24 − 10 = 14. A day has 24 hours, and 10 of them are used for sleep.
maths.context: This is about the 24-hour circle, where you colour in how you spend each hour of one day.
maths.why_maths: Seeing sleep as a part of the whole day shows how much of your life is rest.

maths.problem: Lakshmi measured her height at bedtime: 128.3 cm. In the morning she measured 129.0 cm. How many millimetres taller was she in the morning?
maths.explain: 129.0 − 128.3 = 0.7 centimetres. One centimetre is 10 millimetres, so 0.7 centimetres is 7 millimetres.
maths.context: This is about the taller in the morning test, where you mark your height on a wall at bedtime and again just after waking.
maths.why_maths: The difference is very small, so changing to millimetres makes it easier to see and compare.

maths.problem: In the arm up, arm down test, Divya squeezed 62 times with her arm up and 81 times with her arm down. Her brother squeezed 70 times arm up and 90 times arm down. Did both show the same pattern?
maths.answer: Yes. Both did more squeezes with the arm down: Divya 19 more, her brother 20 more.
maths.explain: 81 − 62 = 19. 90 − 70 = 20. The numbers are different, but both did better with the arm down by about the same amount.
maths.context: This is about the arm up, arm down test, where you squeeze a peg for one minute with your arm raised and then with it hanging down.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the differences, not just the numbers, shows whether two people's results tell the same story.

roots.context: We have learned how muscles get tired and recover, what exercise builds and what happens in sleep. Now we ask what rest tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the peg test, your squeezes slowed each round you did not rest. After two minutes of rest, your count went up again. In those two minutes, your blood brought oxygen and helped the muscle refill its fuel. So a resting muscle is busy, getting ready to work again.
deep_truth.habit: We split the day into working and resting, and think of resting as doing nothing. But the peg test shows that strength comes back during rest, because the body is busy refilling and clearing the muscle.
deep_truth.evidence: The peg count fell from round to round without a break, then rose after two minutes of rest. With the arm held up, so less blood reached the hand, the fingers tired faster.

three.who_am_i: You are a body that works and rests in turns, all day and all night. Even your heart rests for a moment between beats.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing has times of activity and times of rest. A tamarind tree folds their leaves at night, and a dog sleeps and dreams.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth turns from day to night, and the sea comes in and goes out. Much of the world moves in rhythms of more and less.

roots.thread: The peg test showed a rhythm: work uses the fuel up, and rest fills it again. The same rhythm runs through many things. Your heart contracts and then relaxes, every second of your life. Your lungs fill and empty. The Earth turns its face to the Sun and away again. A tamarind tree folds their leaves at night. Your whole body sleeps and wakes. One rhythm of using and refilling shows up in muscles, hearts, trees and planets.

teachings.teaching: Yoga is not for someone who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little. It is for someone who keeps a balance in eating, playing, working, sleeping and waking.
teachings.link: The peg test and the sleep diary both show that the body needs a balance of work and rest, not only one of them.

teachings.teaching: A pose should be steady and comfortable.
teachings.link: In tree pose, your muscles work and relax in tiny amounts, all the time, to keep you steady. Steadiness itself needs a balance of effort and ease.

teachings.teaching: There are four states of awareness: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and a fourth that is aware of all three.
teachings.link: Sleep scientists also find different states in one night: light sleep, deep sleep and dreaming sleep. The Upanishad asks who is aware through all of them.

science.text: After hard work, a muscle refills most of its quick fuel within a few minutes, using oxygen brought by the blood.
The brain is very active in dreaming sleep, and sleep helps people remember what they learned.
Why animals need sleep at all has no full answer yet.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home in a city flat with the materials listed. The tired peg test needs a firm peg: a very soft one may not tire the fingers in five rounds, so the step says to hold two pegs together if needed. The helper counts under their breath, so the child can put all their effort into squeezing. A grown-up repeats the test, because the pattern matters more than the numbers. The arm up, arm down test does the arm-up round first and rests 10 minutes between rounds, so practice cannot explain an arm-down win, and the arm rests against a wall so the shoulder does not give out first. The height test asks for three marks each time and the middle one, because a home tape measure can be a millimetre or two off. It warns that a difference of 1 or 2 millimetres could be a mistake, and suggests measuring a grown-up too. Star jumps in the game become marching on the spot in flats with neighbours below. The sleep diary shows how to count hours across midnight. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many scientists thought sleep was the brain switching off, like a lamp at night. In 1951 Eugene Aserinsky was a student at the University of Chicago, working for the sleep scientist Nathaniel Kleitman. Aserinsky used a machine that recorded the brain's tiny electrical signals, and the movements of the eyes, with wires taped to the head. His first sleeper was his own son, Armond, who was 8 years old. All night the pens of the machine scratched lines on paper. Several times in the night, the lines went wild. Armond's eyes were darting about under his closed lids, and his brain signals looked almost like those of someone awake. At first Aserinsky thought the old machine was broken. But it happened again and again, in other sleepers too, at regular times each night. When sleepers were woken during these times, they usually said they had been dreaming. In 1953 Aserinsky and Kleitman published what they found. They had discovered dreaming sleep, called REM sleep. The brain does not switch off at night.
how_we_found_out.who: Eugene Aserinsky, a student, and Nathaniel Kleitman, a sleep scientist, at the University of Chicago, with Aserinsky's son Armond as the first sleeper
how_we_found_out.when: 1951 to 1953 (published in the journal Science in 1953)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought the brain switches off during sleep, like a lamp. The recordings showed that several times every night the brain becomes almost as active as when awake, and that this is when most vivid dreams happen.
